chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Cost of Getting It Wrong

lessons.title: Interest for Missing or Short-Paying an Instalment

body.text: Interest for deferment is the price of paying late within the year. Each of the four due dates is tested on its own, against the tax you finally declare. Miss June, September or December and you pay three months' interest on that shortfall; miss March and you pay one month. The charge is fixed, predictable and entirely avoidable.

children.text: The previous lesson dealt with not paying enough by the end of the year. This one deals with paying too slowly during it. Section 425 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (old section 234C) looks at each instalment date separately, and it applies even if you pay 100% of your tax by 15 March. This is the interest most taxpayers who "paid everything on time" are surprised by.

markDefs.definition: Tax on the total income declared in your return, reduced by TDS, TCS and any relief. Section 425 measures every instalment against this final figure, not against the estimate you used during the year.

children.text: At each due date, the law compares what you had paid cumulatively with the required percentage of your
. If you are below the floor, you pay 1% a month on the shortfall from the full required percentage, for a fixed number of months.

body.caption: Section 425 at a glance

body.latex: \text{Interest for an instalment} = \text{Shortfall rounded down to the nearest 100 rupees} \times 1\% \times \text{Months}
body.caption: Months are 3 for June, September and December, and 1 for March

body.text: The months charged are fixed. If you miss the June instalment, the interest is three months on that shortfall whether you catch up on 16 June or on 14 September. So the June interest cannot be reduced once 15 June has passed. What a prompt catch-up does protect is the September instalment, which is tested separately.

body.title: Quick Check: Late by Five Days
body.question: Dinesh's tax due on returned income is ₹80,000. He forgets the June instalment and pays ₹12,000 on 20 June 2026, then keeps to every later date. How is his June instalment treated under section 425?
options: No interest, because he paid within the same month
Interest for 3 months on ₹12,000, because nothing had been paid by 15 June
Interest for 1 month, because he was only a few days late
body.explanation: On 15 June he had paid nothing, which is below the 12% floor, so the shortfall is the full 15% of ₹80,000, which is ₹12,000. Interest for June is always 3 months: ₹12,000 × 1% × 3 = ₹360. The payment on 20 June still counts towards his September instalment, which is why it was worth making.

children.text: Last lesson, Nisha, the Indore brand strategist, paid no advance tax on tax due of ₹2,00,000 and settled it all in July. Section 424 charged her ₹8,000. Now add section 425 for the four instalments she missed.

body.title: Show me the math: Nisha's section 425 interest

content.caption: Instalment interest on ₹2,00,000 with nothing paid

children.text: Notice that the March shortfall is the full tax, but only one month of interest is charged on it. The heaviest charge is December, where 75% of the tax is outstanding for three months.

body.label: Total cost of ignoring advance tax on ₹2 lakh
body.context: About 9.0% of her tax, for paying in July instead of on schedule. None of it is deductible, and all of it was avoidable.

body.title: Try It: Two Short Instalments
body.prompt: Harpreet, a Ludhiana-based consultant with regular books, has tax due on returned income of ₹1,00,000. Her cumulative advance tax was ₹10,000 by 15 June, ₹40,000 by 15 September, ₹60,000 by 15 December and ₹1,00,000 by 15 March. What is her total interest under section 425? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: June: 10% is below the 12% floor, so interest is on ₹15,000 minus ₹10,000, which is ₹5,000, for 3 months: ₹150. September: 40% is above the 36% floor, so nil. December: 60% against 75% with no cushion, so ₹15,000 for 3 months: ₹450. March: fully paid, nil. Total ₹600.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The March Instalment
body.textWithBlank: A shortfall in the 15 March instalment attracts interest under section 425 for ___ month.
body.explanation: March is charged for one month, while June, September and December are each charged for three. Amounts are rounded down to the nearest ₹100 first: for example, if tax due is ₹1,43,275 and only ₹10,000 was paid by 15 June, the June shortfall of ₹11,491.25 is taken as ₹11,400, giving ₹342 of interest.

children.text: How the Timing Relief Changes the Numbers

Gautam, a salaried engineer in Pune with fully covered salary TDS, books a short-term gain on 10 October 2026 that creates ₹60,000 of tax with no TDS. Because the gain arose after 15 September, it is left out when testing the June and September instalments. It is included from December. In the return, you give a quarter-wise breakup of capital gains and dividends so that this can be applied.

body.title: Section 425 interest on ₹60,000 of tax, depending on the income type and when it is paid

data.label: Capital gain, tax paid by 15 Dec
Capital gain, tax paid by 15 Mar
Income with no relief, paid by 15 Dec
Income with no relief, paid by 15 Mar

children.text: Paying the tax on his gain by 15 December costs Gautam nothing. Waiting until March costs ₹1,350, the December shortfall for three months. The same ₹60,000 of tax from income with no relief, such as rent or freelance fees earned through the year, would have cost ₹1,080 even if paid in December, and ₹2,430 if left to March.

If you declare income under the presumptive scheme in section 58, the June, September and December tests do not apply. Section 425 checks only whether 100% of tax due on returned income was paid by 15 March, and charges one month on any shortfall. Sameera, the Bengaluru developer from Chapter 2, owes ₹1,66,400. If she pays ₹1,20,000 by 15 March and the rest on 31 March, her section 425 interest is 1% of ₹46,400, which is ₹464. Because the full amount was paid by 31 March, section 424 does not apply.

body.title: You missed an instalment. What now?

columns.label: What you cannot change
points: Interest for the missed instalment is already fixed at 3 months (or 1 for March)
Paying a day or a month after the due date gives the same interest for that instalment
The shortfall is measured against your final tax, not your estimate

columns.label: What you can still protect
points: Catch up before the next due date so that instalment is not short too
Pay at least 90% by 31 March to avoid section 424 interest
Pay tax on any new capital gains or dividends by the very next due date to keep the timing relief

body.text: Paying what you estimated is not a defence. Section 425 tests each instalment against the tax on the income you finally return. If your June estimate was far too low for income that does not get the timing relief, such as freelance or business income, the shortfall is measured against the real figure and interest follows.

body.title: Scenario: Priya Underestimated
body.scenario: Priya is an independent UX researcher in Gurugram who keeps regular books. In June 2026 she estimated advance tax of ₹1,00,000 and dutifully paid 15%, 45% and 75% of that figure on each date: ₹15,000, ₹45,000 and ₹75,000 cumulatively. Work picked up sharply, and by March her tax due on returned income was ₹1,60,000. She paid the full ₹1,60,000 by 15 March 2027.
body.prompt: She paid every instalment on time based on her estimate, and 100% by March. Does she owe interest under section 425 or section 424? Calculate it.
body.modelAnswer: Section 424 does not apply, because she paid 100% of her tax by 15 March. Section 425 does, because each instalment is tested against the final ₹1,60,000. June: the floor is 12%, or ₹19,200, and she paid ₹15,000, so interest is on 15% (₹24,000) minus ₹15,000, which is ₹9,000, for 3 months: ₹270. September: the floor is 36%, or ₹57,600, and she paid ₹45,000, so interest is on 45% (₹72,000) minus ₹45,000, which is ₹27,000, for 3 months: ₹810. December: 75% is ₹1,20,000 and she paid ₹75,000, so ₹45,000 for 3 months: ₹1,350. March: nil. Total ₹2,430. Freelance income does not get the timing relief, so the fix is not to pay more in June but to revise the estimate at each date as work comes in. Had she revised to ₹1,60,000 in September and topped up to 45%, she would have avoided the September and December interest, leaving just the June charge.

body.title: Instalment Interest Prevention Checklist
steps: Before each due date, revise your full-year estimate using actual income to date
Pay at least the full target percentage, treating 12% and 36% as emergency floors only
Pay tax on any capital gain, dividend or winning by the next due date after it arises
Record, quarter by quarter, when capital gains and dividends arose, so the return can apply the timing relief
If you use the presumptive scheme, make sure 100% is paid by 15 March, not 31 March
After filing, check the interest computed in the processing intimation against your own figures

body.label: Section 425: Interest for Deferment of Advance Tax
body.description: Text and explanation of section 425 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, which replaces section 234C of the 1961 Act.

cards.definition: Interest at 1% a month on instalment shortfalls: 3 months each for June, September and December, 1 month for March.
Tax on the income declared in your return, less TDS, TCS and relief. The yardstick for every instalment.
Interest for a missed instalment is the same whether you catch up the next day or just before the next due date.
The return asks when capital gains and dividends arose, so they are excluded from instalments due before that date.
Only the 15 March test applies: 1% for one month on any shortfall from 100%.
Section 424 asks whether 90% was paid by 31 March; section 425 asks whether each instalment was on time. Both can apply.

points: Section 425 tests each due date separately against the tax on the income you finally return
Below the floor, interest is 1% a month on the shortfall from the full required percentage: 3 months for June, September and December, 1 month for March
Interest for a missed instalment is fixed once the date passes, but catching up quickly protects the next instalment
Capital gains, dividends and casual income are excluded from instalments due before they arose, if their tax is paid by the next due date
Presumptive taxpayers face only the 15 March test
Paying on your estimate is not enough if the estimate was too low; revise at every due date

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Section references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025, with the corresponding Income-tax Act, 1961 section in brackets. Examples are simplified and reflect the position as understood at the time of writing. Actual interest is computed by the department when your return is processed. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
